title: Two ways to ask
prompt:
You want an AI to find the hypertensive patients in your data. Which
prompt will get you better code?

**Prompt A**

> Write R code to find the hypertensive patients.

**Prompt B**

> I have a data frame called `visits`. `sbp` and `dbp` are blood pressures
> in mmHg, stored as numbers; `sbp` has one missing value. Write R code
> that keeps patients whose systolic is 140 or more, or whose diastolic is
> 90 or more, and prints how many patients were kept.
hint:
The AI can't see your data, and it can't read your mind. What would it
have to guess from Prompt A?

options.text: B — without it, the AI has to guess the column names, the threshold, and how to handle the missing value
options.feedback:
Right. The AI can't see your data, so everything it isn't told, it
guesses: what the data frame and columns are called, which threshold
counts as hypertensive, whether *either* number being high is enough,
and what to do with a missing reading. Prompt B answers each of those.

It isn't that longer is better. Every sentence in B answers a question
the AI would otherwise answer for you, silently. And the last request
makes the result easy to check.

In practice, you'd rarely write B first time. You'd know about the
missing value only after looking at the data, or after a first attempt
turned it up. That's fine — later in this module you'll see how that
loop goes.

options.text: A — a short prompt leaves the AI free to choose the best approach
options.feedback:
The approach isn't the problem. A leaves the AI to decide things only
you can decide — which threshold, what counts as hypertensive — and to
guess things it can't see, like your column names.

options.text: B — longer prompts always get better code
options.feedback:
B is better, but not because it's longer. It works because each
sentence answers a question the AI would otherwise guess: names,
threshold, and what to do about the missing value.

options.text: No real difference — the AI will work out what's meant
options.feedback:
It will work out *something*, and the code will run. But "hypertensive"
has more than one definition, and the AI will pick one without telling
you. The next exercise shows what that does to the result.

title: Decisions nobody asked for
prompt:
Given Prompt A — *"Write R code to find the hypertensive patients"* — an
AI wrote:

```r
library(dplyr)
hypertensive <- visits |> filter(sbp >= 130 | dbp >= 80)
```

`|` means *or*. Which of the AI's decisions are clinical ones, that should
have been yours? Choose all that apply.
hint:
Some of these change which patients end up in the result. Others only
change how the code looks.
setup:
visits <- data.frame(
  id      = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6),
  age     = c(58, 71, 65, 49, 80, 66),
  sbp     = c(128, 152, NA, 141, 135, 162),
  dbp     = c(82, 94, 88, 91, 76, 99),
  on_meds = c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

options.text: Using 130/80 as the threshold
options.feedback:
A clinical decision. The 2017 American guidelines start hypertension at
130/80; European guidelines use 140/90. Either can be right for your
study — but the AI chose without saying so.

And it matters: on this data, 130/80 flags **all six** patients. At
140/90, it's three. One decision nobody made doubled the count, and
nothing in the code or the output says a decision was made at all.

options.text: Counting a patient if *either* number is high, rather than both
options.feedback:
A clinical decision too, hidden in a single character: `|` means *or*.
With `&`, *and*, fewer patients would qualify.

*Either* happens to be what you wanted here. But the AI decided it
silently, and next time its choice won't necessarily match yours.

options.text: Using dplyr's `filter()` rather than square brackets
options.feedback:
A style choice. Either way of writing it can give the same patients —
this changes how the code looks, not who's in the result.

options.text: Calling the result `hypertensive`
options.feedback: Just a name. It doesn't change which patients are in the result.

title: Write the prompt
prompt:
You want the average systolic pressure for patients on medication, and for
patients not on medication. Here's what `str(visits)` shows:

```
'data.frame':  6 obs. of  5 variables:
 $ id     : num  1 2 3 4 5 6
 $ age    : num  58 71 65 49 80 66
 $ sbp    : num  128 152 NA 141 135 162
 $ dbp    : num  82 94 88 91 76 99
 $ on_meds: logi  FALSE TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE TRUE
```

Write the prompt you'd give an AI. Two things go in it:

- **Have** — what the data looks like: names, what the values are, any
  quirks
- **Want** — exactly what you need back, including any decisions only you
  can make

The third part, **Check**, is yours: how you'll know the answer is right.
It helps to ask the code to *print* things you can check — R computes
those, not the AI.
hint:
Which columns does the task need? What kind of values are in each? Is
anything missing that could affect an average — and what should happen to
it?

response.exemplar:
There's a column called sbp, with numbers and one missing value, and a
column called on_meds that is TRUE or FALSE. Write R code that gives the
mean sbp for patients with on_meds TRUE, and another for on_meds FALSE.
Leave out missing values, and have the code print how many values each
mean is based on.

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt name every column the task needs? (It needs a systolic pressure column, plus a column saying whether each patient is on medication.)
rubric.on_fail:
**Have:** name the columns the task needs. The AI can't see your data,
so it will guess what they're called — and a wrong guess either fails
or, worse, quietly uses the wrong column.

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt say what kind of values those columns hold — for example, numbers in mmHg, or TRUE/FALSE?
rubric.on_fail:
**Have:** say what's *in* the columns — numbers in mmHg, TRUE or FALSE.
The AI writes different code for numbers than for text, and it can't
tell which you have.

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt say what should happen to the missing systolic value?
rubric.on_fail:
**Want:** one systolic reading is missing. Say what should happen to
it — left out, or something else. If you don't, the AI decides, and a
missing value can turn an entire average into `NA` or vanish without
a word.

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt ask the code to print something the writer could check against the data themselves — such as how many values each average is based on?
rubric.on_fail:
**Check:** ask the code to print something you can verify yourself.
How many values each average is based on is a good one — R counts
them, and you can count them in the data. (Asking the AI to *tell* you
it worked isn't a check: it hasn't run anything on your data.)

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt ask for an average for each medication group — patients on medication, as well as patients not on medication?
rubric.on_fail:
**Want:** the task needs two averages — one for patients on
medication, one for patients not on it. Ask for each, or the AI will
give you only what you asked for.

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt stick to the columns this task uses, rather than listing every column in the data?
rubric.on_fail:
**Enough, and no more:** this task only uses the systolic and
medication columns. Listing every column does no harm here, but it's
a habit worth breaking — in real data, column names can give away more
about your work than you'd think.

title: The best follow-up
prompt:
The AI hands you code. Which follow-up is most likely to show you what
could be wrong with it?
hint:
Which question does the AI have the least incentive to answer with
"yes, it's fine"?

options.text: "List every decision this code makes that I didn't specify."
options.feedback:
Right. This asks for exactly what you can't easily see: the gaps the
AI filled — a threshold, how missing values are handled, which rows
are kept. Once they're listed, you can check each against what you
meant.

But treat the list as a starting point, not a guarantee. An AI can't
list a decision it doesn't realise it made — `cut()`'s boundary, in the
next exercise, is a good example. The list tells you where to look;
testing tells you what's true.

options.text: "Is this code correct?"
options.feedback:
This invites reassurance. AI models lean towards agreeing with you,
and "correct" can only mean "matches what you asked" — so anything you
didn't specify, it can't flag as wrong. Asking for the decisions it
made gets you further.

options.text: "Make this code better."
options.feedback:
You'll get *different* code, but "better" isn't something you can check.
The new version may make new decisions you didn't ask for.

options.text: "Explain this code line by line."
options.feedback:
Useful for learning what the code does. But it explains what's there,
not what's *missing* — the decisions you never made won't stand out
unless you ask for them directly.

title: Something you've never seen
prompt:
You asked for an age-group column — under 65, and 65 and over. The AI
wrote this, using a function you haven't met:

```r
visits$age_group <- cut(visits$age, breaks = c(0, 65, Inf),
                        labels = c("under 65", "65 and over"))
```

It looks right. Use the routine for anything unfamiliar: **name it** (what
might `cut()` do?), **look it up** if you like, then **try it on something
small where you know the answer**. Run this in the box above it:

```r
cut(c(64, 65, 66), breaks = c(0, 65, Inf),
    labels = c("under 65", "65 and over"))
```

Which group does a 65-year-old land in?
hint: Run it and read the middle value.
setup:
visits <- data.frame(
  id      = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6),
  age     = c(58, 71, 65, 49, 80, 66),
  sbp     = c(128, 152, NA, 141, 135, 162),
  dbp     = c(82, 94, 88, 91, 76, 99),
  on_meds = c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

options.text: "under 65"
options.feedback:
Right — and almost nobody would guess it. `cut()` makes groups that
include their *upper* boundary by default, so 65 falls into the group
that ends at 65. Patient 3, aged exactly 65, would be labelled "under
65". Adding `right = FALSE` moves the boundary the other way.

Nothing in the code, the name, or a quick read would tell you that.
Trying it on a value that sits exactly on the boundary does. Boundaries
are where code most often disagrees quietly with a clinical
definition, so they're always worth one test.

options.text: "65 and over"
options.feedback:
That's what the labels say, and what you'd expect. Run the line above
it and look at the middle value: `cut()` puts 65 in "under 65".

options.text: `NA` — it falls between the groups
options.feedback:
It does land in a group. Run the line and look at the middle value — 
it's not the group you'd expect.

title: A whole script at once
prompt:
An AI hands you a 40-line script in five steps: read the data, clean it,
add a column, filter it, and summarise it. What's the best way to use it?
hint: If the final number is wrong, how would you find out which step went wrong?

options.text: Run it one step at a time, checking each result before the next
options.feedback:
Right. If you only check the end, a wrong answer could have come from
any of five places — and a *plausible* wrong answer wouldn't send you
looking at all. Checking each step as you go catches a problem where
it starts.

Notice what this means: how much code you *ask for* and how often you
*check* are separate choices. You can take a whole script at once and
still run it in pieces.

options.text: Run all of it, then check the final number
options.feedback:
If the number looks wrong, you won't know which of the five steps
caused it. And if it looks *right* but isn't, you won't look at all.
Checking each step catches a problem where it starts.

options.text: Ask the AI to give it to you one line at a time instead
options.feedback:
That works — and in unfamiliar territory it can be worth it. But it's
slow, and you don't need it to check as you go: you can take the whole
script and still *run* it one step at a time.

options.text: Read it carefully, then run it all
options.feedback:
Reading helps, but many problems don't show on the page — a column
stored as text, a missing value, a boundary. Running each step and
looking at what it produced shows what reading can't.

title: When the whole thing is fine
prompt:
Checking every step isn't always worth the time. In which of these is it
reasonable to take a whole script and check only the end result?
hint: When would a wrong result be obvious at a glance?

options.text: Remaking a kind of plot you've made many times before
options.feedback:
Right. You know what it should look like, so a mistake shows at a
glance, and little rides on it. Checking step by step pays off when
you *can't* tell a wrong answer from a right one by looking — new data,
new tools, numbers that matter.

options.text: The first analysis of a dataset you haven't looked at yet
options.feedback:
This is where step-by-step matters most. You don't yet know the data's
quirks — text in a number column, a value in the wrong unit — and each
step is a chance for one to slip through.

options.text: Numbers that will go into a paper or a report
options.feedback:
The higher the stakes, the more it's worth checking each step. A
plausible wrong number in a paper is exactly what you're trying to
avoid.

options.text: Code that uses a package you've never used
options.feedback:
New tools are where surprises live — like `cut()` putting 65 in the
wrong group. Step by step, with small tests, is the safer way here.

title: Rewrite a weak prompt
prompt:
Someone asked an AI:

> Add a column for high blood pressure.

Rewrite it so the AI has nothing important left to guess. You want each
patient labelled "high" or "not high", using 140/90, where either number
being high is enough. Here's the data again:

```
'data.frame':  6 obs. of  5 variables:
 $ id     : num  1 2 3 4 5 6
 $ age    : num  58 71 65 49 80 66
 $ sbp    : num  128 152 NA 141 135 162
 $ dbp    : num  82 94 88 91 76 99
 $ on_meds: logi  FALSE TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE TRUE
```

Use **Have** and **Want** — and ask for output you can check yourself.
hint:
Which decisions did the original leave to the AI? There are at least three
— and one patient's systolic is missing.

response.exemplar:
I have a data frame called visits, with systolic (sbp) and diastolic (dbp)
blood pressure in mmHg, stored as numbers. sbp has one missing value. Add
a column called bp_status that says "high" if sbp is 140 or more OR dbp
is 90 or more, and "not high" otherwise. If sbp is missing, decide using
dbp alone. Have the code print how many patients are labelled "high",
and list any decisions you made that I didn't specify.

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt name the blood pressure columns the code should use?
rubric.on_fail:
**Have:** name the columns — the AI can't see them. Without names, it
guesses.

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt give the threshold as specific numbers — 140 systolic, 90 diastolic?
rubric.on_fail:
**Want:** give the numbers. "High blood pressure" has more than one
definition, and the AI will choose one for you — 130/80 flagged every
patient in this data.

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt make clear that either number being high is enough (systolic OR diastolic)?
rubric.on_fail:
**Want:** say whether *either* number being high is enough, or both
must be. That one word changes who's included.

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt say what should happen when the systolic value is missing?
rubric.on_fail:
**Want:** one patient's systolic is missing. Say what should happen —
otherwise the AI decides, and that patient may quietly get the wrong
label, or none.

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt ask the code to print something the writer could check themselves, such as how many patients are labelled high?
rubric.on_fail:
**Check:** ask the code to print something you can verify — how many
patients end up "high" is a good one. Then compare it with your own
count. Keep the number you expect to yourself.

title: Telling it the answer
prompt:
You've counted by hand: three patients should come out as high. Should you
put that in your prompt — *"I expect three patients"*?
hint:
A check works because it's independent of the thing it checks. Would it
still be?

options.text: No — keep it to yourself, and compare it with what the code prints
options.feedback:
Right. A check only works if it's independent of what it's checking.
If the AI knows the answer you expect, it may write code that reaches
that number rather than the right one — and then a match tells you
nothing.

So the check stays yours — and it isn't redoing R's work. It's a quick
spot-check: do the counts add up to the total? Does one patient you
know land where they should? Is the number plausible? Work it out
however suits you — pen and paper, or a few throwaway lines in the
console — ideally before you see the AI's result, so it can't nudge
you.

Having the code print a count is fine, whether the AI writes that line
or you type it into the console yourself: R computes it. What isn't a
check is the AI *telling* you the result is right.

options.text: Yes — it helps the AI get the right answer
options.feedback:
It helps the AI get *your* answer, which isn't the same thing. If your
count is wrong, or the AI bends the code to match it, the two agree
and nothing looks amiss. Keep the expected answer to yourself and
compare afterwards.

options.text: Yes — then the AI can check its own work
options.feedback:
An AI writing code in a chat hasn't run it on your data. When it says
"this gives three", it's predicting, not checking — and it can be
confidently wrong. Even an AI tool that runs code can't see your real
data, so it would be checking against its own guess of what your data
looks like.

title: What belongs in the prompt
prompt:
You're asking an AI to label each patient's blood pressure. The less you
share, the less can leak — about your patients, and about an idea you
haven't published yet. But leave out something the code depends on, and
the AI guesses.

Which of these belong in the prompt? Choose all that apply.
hint: For each one, ask: would the code be different without it?

options.text: The names of the blood pressure columns, and that they hold numbers in mmHg
options.feedback:
Belongs. The code can't be written without the names, and numbers need
different code from text.

If your real names would give your idea away, placeholders work just as
well. Just remember you're now showing a stand-in: when the code comes
back, map each name back carefully, because a mix-up there is a silent
error of its own.

options.text: That one systolic value is missing
options.feedback:
Belongs. A missing value changes what the code has to do, and it's
exactly the kind of thing an AI won't assume.

options.text: The threshold you want to use
options.feedback:
Belongs. It's a clinical decision, and if you leave it out, the AI
makes it for you.

options.text: What your study is trying to show
options.feedback:
Leave it out. It doesn't change a line of the code — and it's the part
of your work someone else could take.

options.text: Each patient's actual readings
options.feedback:
Leave them out. The AI needs the *shape* of the data, not the values;
the values are what you're protecting. Describe a simple dataset shaped
like yours instead — placeholder names are fine — as long as it's still
representative. If the real data has a missing value, say so, or the
code won't handle it. Module 16 is about exactly this.

options.text: Which hospital the data came from
options.feedback:
Leave it out. It changes nothing in the code, and it narrows down
whose data this is.

title: Something you didn't know to mention
prompt:
Real prompting is rarely right first time. You asked an AI to label each
patient "high" or "not high" at 140/90, either number counting. It wrote:

```r
visits$bp_status <- ifelse(visits$sbp >= 140 | visits$dbp >= 90,
                           "high", "not high")
table(visits$bp_status)
```

`table()` counts how many times each label appears. It printed:

```
    high not high
       3        2
```

That's five patients. There are six. Run `summary(visits)` in the box above
to find out why — it's something you didn't know when you wrote the prompt.

What's the best next message to the AI?
hint:
Look at the `NA's` line for `sbp`. Then ask: what does the AI need to know,
and what does it need you to decide?
setup:
visits <- data.frame(
  id      = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6),
  age     = c(58, 71, 65, 49, 80, 66),
  sbp     = c(128, 152, NA, 141, 135, 162),
  dbp     = c(82, 94, 88, 91, 76, 99),
  on_meds = c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

options.text: "One sbp value is missing, so that patient got no label. When sbp is missing, decide using dbp alone."
options.feedback:
Right. It says what you found and what you've decided. Patient 3's
systolic is missing, so the comparison came out as `NA` and they got no
label at all — and `table()` quietly leaves missing labels out of its
count. The only clue was that three plus two isn't six.

This is how prompting usually goes: ask, run, check, discover
something, and say exactly what you found. You couldn't have mentioned
the missing value up front without looking first — and looking first,
with `str()` or `summary()`, is often worth doing. But some things only
turn up once you check, and that's a normal part of the work, not a
failure.

options.text: "The count is wrong. Please fix it."
options.feedback:
The AI doesn't know what you found, so it has to guess what "wrong"
means — and it might change something that was fine. Say what you
discovered — a missing systolic — and what should happen to it.

options.text: Paste the data into the chat so the AI can see the problem for itself
options.feedback:
That's patient data, and it shouldn't go into a prompt. You don't need
to share it: you've already found the problem with `summary()`. Tell the
AI what you found, in words.

options.text: Accept the result — one patient won't change much
options.feedback:
That patient has no label at all, so any count or percentage that uses
this column is quietly based on five patients, not six. And the
decision about what to do with them is a clinical one — it should be
yours.

title: A step you can write yourself
prompt:
Finding the hypertensive patients breaks into small steps. The first:
make a column that's TRUE when a patient's systolic is 140 or more, *or*
their diastolic is 90 or more.

A step this small you can write yourself — no AI needed. `|` means *or*.
Write it, press **Run**, then look at the new column with
`visits$high_bp`.
hint:
A comparison on a whole column gives one TRUE or FALSE per patient. Make
one for `sbp` and one for `dbp`, and join them with `|`.
setup:
visits <- data.frame(
  id      = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6),
  age     = c(58, 71, 65, 49, 80, 66),
  sbp     = c(128, 152, NA, 141, 135, 162),
  dbp     = c(82, 94, 88, 91, 76, 99),
  on_meds = c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

solution.why:
Look at the result: `FALSE TRUE NA TRUE FALSE TRUE`. Patient 3 is `NA`,
because their systolic is missing. One small step, one look, and the
missing value has shown itself — before it could hide inside a count
later on.

That's why small steps pay off. Each is easy to check, and many are
easy to write yourself. The next step — keeping the TRUE rows and
counting them — is one line too, and now you know to decide what
happens to patient 3 first.

Save the AI for the steps you can't write. Asking it for one you can
is usually slower, and you understand your own code better than its.

checks.expr: identical(visits$high_bp, c(FALSE, TRUE, NA, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE))
checks.on_fail:
Not quite yet. Run your line and look at `visits$high_bp` — you should
see one TRUE or FALSE per patient.

match.expr: identical(visits$high_bp, c(FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE))

misconceptions.feedback:
That's `&`, *and* — both numbers high. The task says *either*, which is
`|`. In this data the two happen to agree for every patient except
patient 3, which is exactly what makes the slip so easy to miss.
Store it as a column in the data frame: `visits$high_bp <- …`.

TRUE or FALSE is all this step needs — no labels. A comparison gives
you that directly.
